analysis.one_liner: Narrows which waters federal clean-water law covers and pays landowners double for lost property value.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by three Republican senators, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in December 2018 and never received a hearing or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would sharply limit which waters fall under the Clean Water Act, excluding most wetlands, intermittent streams, drainage channels, and groundwater unless they directly connect to navigable water. It would also void existing federal rules defining those waters, ban agencies from interpreting the definition without new congressional action, require landowner written consent before federal inspectors enter private property, and require federal agencies to pay landowners twice the appraised loss when a water rule lowers their property's value. States would remain free to regulate waters themselves.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of land containing wetlands or seasonal streams — especially developers, builders, agricultural operations, and mining or energy interests — who could fill, drain, or build on those areas without federal Clean Water Act permits, inspections, or agency jurisdiction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, large landowners, and extractive industries

how_it_helps.text: It excludes from federal jurisdiction wetlands without a continuous surface connection to covered waters, intermittent and rain-drainage channels, and groundwater, removing the need for federal permits to alter them.

It bars the use of the 'significant nexus' test that had allowed regulators to assert jurisdiction over waters connected ecologically rather than physically, and blocks 'aggregation' of wetlands to claim federal control.

It voids the 1986 and 2015 federal rules and 2008 guidance defining 'waters of the United States,' and prohibits agencies from issuing any new interpretation of the definition without explicit congressional authorization.
It grants property owners expedited judicial review, within 30 days, of any jurisdictional determination affecting their land use, in a federal court located in their own state.

It requires federal agencies to pay affected landowners twice the appraised fair-market loss from any navigable-waters regulation, and such a regulation has no force until every landowner claim is paid.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people downstream: reduced federal oversight of wetlands and intermittent streams can degrade the waters that feed drinking supplies and absorb floodwater, and taxpayers fund the double compensation payments out of agency operating budgets. Water quality enforcement shifts to states with varying capacity and willingness.
analysis.who_pays_short: Downstream communities, water users, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Wetlands and seasonal streams excluded from federal jurisdiction filter pollution, store floodwater, and recharge aquifers; removing them from Clean Water Act coverage leaves drinking water sources and flood-prone communities more exposed, with protection depending on each state's own rules.

The double-compensation requirement, paid from agency general operating funds, could drain resources from the very agencies responsible for water quality, and a regulation cannot take effect until all landowner claims are paid, letting a single unresolved claim stall a rule.

Prohibiting any federal agency interpretation of the definition without new congressional action would make water rules effectively frozen, leaving enforcement to fit future science and circumstances into a static statutory text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For large landowners and developers, the bill delivers a real and immediate benefit: fewer federal permits, inspections, and liability costs. For the broader public, the cost is weaker protection for the smaller waters and wetlands that feed and clean the water systems people depend on, plus a taxpayer-funded compensation obligation at double the actual loss. States would keep authority to regulate, so the outcome depends heavily on how aggressively each state chooses to act.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 17, 2018, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on December 17, 2018, with Sens. Ted Cruz and Chuck Grassley as cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where no further action was recorded.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, existing federal definitions of protected waters remained in force, so downstream communities and water users kept the stronger status quo; landowners and developers who sought the looser rules gained nothing in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downstream communities and current water rules

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case for narrowing federal water jurisdiction and compensating landowners.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it stayed there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would remove federal permitting hurdles for filling or building on wetlands and seasonal streams, cutting their costs. The public bears the tradeoff in reduced protection for the waters and wetlands that supply drinking water and absorb floods.

Farm operations dealing with drainage ditches, seasonal ponds, and wet patches of land would largely fall outside federal Clean Water Act jurisdiction, along with eased restrictions on federal site entry. The cost falls on water quality downstream.

Removing ephemeral streams and groundwater from federal jurisdiction would ease permitting for operations that affect small or seasonal waterways, with pollution and water-use consequences for nearby communities.

industries.industry: Water utilities and downstream water users
industries.note: Weaker federal protection for headwater streams and wetlands can raise treatment costs and water quality risks for the utilities and communities that depend on those sources.
